title: One World, Many Peoples
intro: Menchú's opening case, what indigenous means, and the shared colonial wound.

terms.def: Originating in a place. George Manuel's definition covers peoples living in their traditional homelands across every continent.
Judging other peoples by your own culture's standards, the attitude underneath colonial policy everywhere.

body: The chapter opens with a voice, not a definition. Rigoberta Menchú Tum, a Maya refugee of Guatemala's thirty-six-year civil war, told interviewer Anders Riis-Hansen that celebrating the 500th anniversary of the discovery of America is the absolute expression of triumphism, occupation, and presumptuousness, then pivoted to what the anniversary unlocked: 1993 declared the International Year of Indigenous Peoples, the first such year in 500, won by untitled, unnamed brothers who patiently walked the corridors. She argues the way this theme will ask you to argue, specific examples tied to specific action.

Indigenous means originating naturally in a region, and identity follows the origin: peoples descended from their lands' original inhabitants, naming themselves simply the people in language after language, Ainu, Dene, Inuit, Maori, Yup'ik. At least 5,000 indigenous cultures hold some 300 million people across seventy countries, and Secwepemc Grand Chief George Manuel, first president of the World Council of Indigenous Peoples, found the pattern on 1970s travels through Argentina, Sweden, Chile, Nicaragua, Guatemala, and Peru: nearly every people wove the four sacred directions and the circle into ceremony. Spirituality braided into land and daily cycles, oral traditions carrying law and memory, from Australian story maps tracing spirit ancestors along rivers and mountains, extended families as social safety nets, and pre-contact territories that respected difference without matching any country's borders.

The shared wound matches the shared culture. Contact with colonizers collapsed populations through war and disease: twenty-five million dead in Spain's sixteenth-century conquest of South and Central America, Caribbean peoples nearly eliminated by the 1890s, Australia's Aboriginal population falling from half a million or more to 60,000, New Zealand's Maori from 200,000 to 42,000. Underneath sat ethnocentrism, judging every culture by your own standards and reading difference as inferiority, dangerous in anyone's hands and devastating when the ethnocentric group holds political and economic power to impose its way of life. Edmonton's Rossdale Flats, a burial and gathering place for thousands of years now threatened by a power-plant expansion, shows the attitude still operating at home.

Common histories produce nine common issues the chapter will tour: land and resources, the environment, war, language and culture, education, self-determination, health, human rights, and intellectual property. Many carry a geopolitical edge, borders slicing ancestral lands so Blackfoot and Mohawk nations straddle the Canada-US line and Inuit live in four countries. Hold the focus questions beside that list as you read: shared characteristics, shared issues, resource development's effects, the UN's role, progress on rights and education, and the youth who inherit all of it.

example.title: See it in the theme
example.text: Pair this lesson with the Halfbreed excerpt in your resources: Campbell's Métis story is one local telling of the worldwide pattern Manuel found, and Menchú's example-plus-action method is the method 4.2 and 4.3 will demand.

check.prompt: What makes very different peoples recognizably Indigenous in the chapter's account?
check.sample: Sample response: originating in their homelands, shared symbols like the circle and four directions, parallel colonial histories of collapse and survival, and the nine common issues those histories produced.

title: Nine Issues, One Pattern
intro: From Java's transmigrants to Shell's human rights policy: the issues tour.

terms.def: Combining geography and politics, as when borders drawn across ancestral lands split indigenous nations.
The 1980s Inuit body spanning four countries, fighting pollution and warming while defending Arctic culture.

body: Land first, because everything else stands on it. Nearly all indigenous peoples fight to regain ancestral and sacred ground or a fair share of its wealth, against governments that reclaim even designated land: Indonesia's 1969 transmigration program moved up to ten million crowded Javanese onto other islands' indigenous territories over three decades, killing hundreds, displacing settlers and hosts alike, and leaving 400,000 people in resettlement camps. Cree youth leader Melina Laboucan-Massimo, coordinating TakingITGlobal across Latin America while studying Indigenous Governance, turns that frustration into method: keep culture intact and integral, resist ethnocentric assimilation, and act.

The tour moves fast, so track the mechanism in each stop. Environment: miners, loggers, and road builders invade Yanomamo territory in Venezuela and Brazil with attacks, disease, and wrecked food supply while neither government defends them. War: Guatemala's civil war killed some 200,000 people, most indigenous, drove hundreds of thousands of Mayans from home, and erased 440 villages. Language and culture: over 2,000 western-hemisphere languages and cultures, Wappo, Beothuk, Takelma, Natchez, Massachuset among them, vanished since 1492, and of 6,000 indigenous languages spoken today many are nearly extinct. Education: half of indigenous Mexicans cannot read or write and 58 percent of their five-year-olds miss school entirely. Self-determination: development under one's own authority, as Greenland's 1979 Home Rule Act granted Inuit domestic autonomy inside Denmark.

Health, rights, and knowledge close the nine. Central Australian indigenous toddlers hospitalize for respiratory illness at 40 percent with triple the infant death rate, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians die twenty years earlier than other Australians, 53 percent before fifty against 13 percent. Human rights law itself did violence: Australia stole about 100,000 indigenous children between the 1870s and 1969 to erase a distinct people, while Canada confined First Nations behind passes and permits, withheld the vote until 1960, and traded land for rights. Intellectual property bleeds quietly as corporations profit from traditional knowledge and artifacts without sharing the wealth.

Protection exists but leaks, which is the lesson's turn. Mechanisms abound yet apply inconsistently, and many peoples never learn their rights, so organization becomes the remedy: shared legal tactics for land claims, treaty enforcement, and the right to live as they choose. The Inuit Circumpolar Conference, founded in the 1980s with national offices in the United States, Canada, Greenland, and Russia plus Sámi concerns in Norway, fights pollution and warming as cultural defense, joined by an alphabet of allies from the Asia Indigenous Peoples Pact to the World Council of Indigenous Peoples. And pressure works: after Nigeria executed Ogoni poet Ken Saro-Wiwa with eight fellow activists for opposing Shell's ecological ruin, worldwide protest forced the oil giant to write human rights into its business plan. Nakoda dancer Cherith Mark offers the same moral in motion, powwow at five to Banff stages, carrying Morley to the world and bringing the world, including Maori genealogy-chanting and Colombian technique, back to teach.

example.title: Pick your organization
example.text: Choose one protection body from this lesson, the ICC, the Indian Law Resource Center, the International Indian Treaty Council, or another, and draft its oral report: mission, history, one accomplishment. Precision beats admiration.

check.prompt: Why do protection mechanisms fail even where they exist?
check.sample: Sample response: they apply inconsistently, many peoples never learn their rights, and enforcement needs organization, which is why shared legal tactics and bodies like the ICC matter.
